first_impression.reaction: Okay, the first sentence actually answers me: prosidba, collecting the bride, crowns and a shared cup, the welcome at her new home. No pop-up, no life story. Key takeaways are right there under it, so I stayed. The title is a bit clickbaity though, 'You Did Not Know?' sounds like a listicle, and the page is not one.

journey.quote: A Serbian wedding is less a single ceremony than a sequence: a visit to ask for the bride's hand, a party sent to collect her, a church service with crowns and a shared cup, and a welcome at her new home.
journey.reaction: That's the answer in one line. Exactly what I wanted on the train.

journey.quote: The kum is the first of two church witnesses and exchanges the rings, a far larger role than the English "best man" suggests.
journey.reaction: Useful, I didn't know that. This is the kind of thing I'd tell a friend.

journey.quote: Smartraveller rates Serbia "Exercise normal safety precautions" as at November 2026, and paperwork for a legal wedding there should be checked with the registry and the Australian Embassy in Belgrade.
journey.reaction: Why is travel safety one of the four takeaways? I asked about traditions. I'd rather see the apple, the kolo or buying back the bride here. The date is nice though, at least I know it's current.

journey.quote: What Are the Serbian Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
journey.reaction: Slightly gimmicky. The H2 underneath, 'Serbian wedding traditions: what the day looks like, in order', is much clearer and matches what I typed.

journey.section: 4. Collecting the bride, and buying her back
journey.quote: It is theatre, not commerce, and the haggling is the point.
journey.reaction: Ha, nice. Short and clear, fun to read.

journey.quote: When the svatovi arrive, the bride's family is often told to "sell" her rather than simply hand her over. The dever, usually the groom's brother or a close male relative, is often told as the one who negotiates.
journey.reaction: 'Often told' twice in two sentences. I get they're being careful, but by the tenth time it reads mushy and I start wondering if they actually know. Fine once in the framing paragraph, too much after that.

journey.quote: UNESCO inscribed "Kolo, traditional folk dance" for Serbia on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2017.
journey.reaction: Specific, dated and sourced. That's what makes me trust it more than a random listicle.

journey.quote: As it is often told, an apple is set high and the groom or his party tries to hit it before the bride is led out.
journey.reaction: The FAQ is good for skimming. These are the exact questions I'd have. I'd probably just read this bit next time.

unanswered_questions: Is there a quick list of all the traditions near the top? I had to scroll through numbered headings on my phone to see them all.
What does the kum's apple, the barjak or the welcome bread actually symbolise? Several sections just say ask your family.

turn_offs_found.why: Takes a quarter of the Key takeaways for something off-topic for someone searching traditions.

turn_offs_found.quote: What Are the Serbian Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
turn_offs_found.why: Clickbait-style title, and it doesn't quite match my search the way the first H2 does.

would_share_with: A friend going to a Serbian wedding as a guest

cta_reaction.quote: If you are planning a Serbian wedding abroad, or a blended celebration in Australia, you can speak with a Wedded Advisor.
cta_reaction.why: I'm not planning a wedding, I just wanted to know what the traditions are. The CTA is calm and doesn't get in my way, which I appreciate. Nothing pushy.

top_3_changes: Replace the Smartraveller Key takeaway with a traditions one (e.g. the apple, buying back the bride or the kolo) and leave travel advice to its own section.
Cut most of the repeated 'often told' after the framing paragraph; say it once per section at most.
Make the title match the query plainly, e.g. along the lines of the first H2, rather than 'You Did Not Know?'.
